# Incident Report — MTA 2026-01-31 Traffic Analysis Exercise

## Evidence reviewed
Only one artifact was present in the evidence directory: `2026-01-31-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (51,181 frames, 26.4 MB, capture window 2026-01-28 03:04:03–03:14:27 UTC, ~624s). No IDS/Suricata alert exports or other artifacts were provided, so no signature-based attribution is possible — everything below is behavioral analysis of the raw traffic.

## Victim host
| Field | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | **10.1.21.58** | Source of all suspicious activity; sole non-DC/non-gateway local host generating traffic |
| MAC | **00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2** | Ethernet source on every frame from 10.1.21.58; confirmed via ARP replies (`arp.src.proto_ipv4==10.1.21.58` → same MAC) |
| Hostname | **DESKTOP-ES9F3ML** | NBNS name registration from 10.1.21.58: `DESKTOP-ES9F3ML<00>` (Workstation), `DESKTOP-ES9F3ML<20>` (Server service); also NetBIOS domain `WIN11OFFICE` |
| AD domain | win11office.com (DC = WIN-LU4L24X3UB7.win11office.com, 10.1.21.2, MAC 14:b3:1f:2d:ce:69) | LDAP/CLDAP/Kerberos traffic between 10.1.21.58 and 10.1.21.2 |
| Logged-in user | **gwyatt** | Kerberos `CNameString = gwyatt`, realm `WIN11OFFICE.COM`, in AS-REQ/TGS-REQ traffic from 10.1.21.58 |

Gateway 10.1.21.1 (MAC 00:04:c1:be:8c:d4) is benign infrastructure.

## Malware family and attribution
**Attribution confidence: behavioral, not signature-confirmed** (no alert data was supplied for cross-reference).

The traffic shows a classic SEO-poisoning / fake-file-hub delivery chain into a browser-fingerprinting loader/C2 check-in:

1. **t=45.1s** — victim issues a `www.google.com` TLS session (search).
2. **t=45.3s** — DNS resolves `hiyter.com` → 104.21.22.231, immediately followed by TLS to it (ECH-masked SNI, small 8 KB exchange) — the redirector/landing page.
3. **t=45.8–46.0s** — DNS resolves `media.megafilehub4.lat` → 104.21.48.156, TLS session opened (217 KB exchanged) — fake file-hosting domain.
4. **t=47.8s** — `cdnjs.cloudflare.com` loaded (page asset for the fake site).
5. **t=48.3s** — DNS resolves `arch.filemegahab4.sbs` → 104.21.46.67, followed immediately by a single TLS session (`10.1.21.58:54840 <-> 104.21.46.67:443`) that transfers **16 MB inbound over 22.4 seconds** — consistent with a malware payload/installer download. TLS 1.3 + Encrypted Client Hello prevented recovery of the URI or file name, so no hash could be extracted.
6. **t=90–103s** — victim begins repeated, short-lived beacon connections to `whitepepper.su` (153.92.1.49) on both port 80 and 443, including explicit plaintext HTTP GETs enumerating installed browsers with a bot ID and token:
   - `GET /api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome`
   - same with `agent=Edge` and `&act=log` variants
   This id/token/agent check-in pattern, followed by dozens of short repeating TLS sessions to the same host, is characteristic of a stealer/loader phoning home and fingerprinting the browsers on the box before further exfiltration.
7. **t=90.3s, 122.8s, 126.5s** — additional connections to `whooptm.cyou` (62.72.32.156), `holiday-forever.cc` (80.97.160.24), and `communicationfirewall-security.cc` (104.21.9.36) — same TTL/TLD pattern (cheap gTLDs .cyou/.cc/.sbs/.lat/.su), likely additional C2/redirector infrastructure for the same campaign.

Given the download-then-browser-fingerprint-beacon sequence, this behaviorally matches a **pay-per-install (PPI) style loader delivering a browser-targeting stealer**. I cannot name the exact family with confidence since no signature/alert data was available and the payload itself was TLS-encrypted.
